attempts.raw_response: The lawyer indicated that the PPS would respond to the defence application in due course. The case relates to the death of a man during the Troubles in Belfast. The HET, established to review legacy cases from the Northern Ireland conflict, had examined the circumstances surrounding the fatal shooting. Defence lawyers for the soldiers argued that their clients should be granted anonymity due to concerns about their safety and the passage of time since the events in question. The proceedings were being closely watched as one of the few cases where former soldiers face criminal charges for Troubles-related killings. Judge Mr. Justice O'Hara presiding over the case set a further hearing date for arguments on the anonymity application to be heard.

pair.human_continuation: District Judge Fiona Bagnall agreed to impose a temporary ban on identifying either ex-soldier under the terms of the Human Rights Act and contempt of court legislation. She stressed that this was merely a "holding position", with the press free to mount a challenge when the case is reviewed again on 20 December. It also emerged that Soldier A and Soldier C will contest that they have a case to answer over the alleged murder. According to the prosecution, Soldier A and Soldier C are surviving members of the Army patrol involved in the shooting incident. A third member of the unit has since died. Joe McCann's widow, Anne, said there were three incontrovertible facts about his death.
pair.prefix: In 2013, the Historical Enquiries Team (HET) concluded that the killing was not justified. Files were passed to the Public Prosecution Service (PPS). It reviewed the case and decided in 2016 that the two soldiers should be charged with murder. A lawyer for the PPS confirmed to Belfast Magistrates' Court that the ex-soldiers were seeking anonymity. "The Crown at this stage has not finalised its position on such an application," he said.
